Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record--For the Appellant. 

Shafiq Ahmed, Senior Advocate (Tabarak Hossain, Advocate with him) instructed by AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record---For the Respondent No. 1.

parties:
Ruhul Amin ------ Appellant
vs
Official Liquidator, Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and proforma defendant No. 6 who filed joint affidavit in opposition contending, inter alia, that the suit property actually appertained to original Jote No. 88/88 of Mouza East Nasirabad, which was created in Settlement Case No. 284 of 1907-1908 in favour of Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, and the said jote comprised the lands of CS Plot Nos. 1609, 1736 and 1748 and on 29-11-1912 Aparna Charan, filed an application before the Khashmahal Office for demarcation of the said jote land which was registered as Judicial Miscellaneous Case (JM Case) No. 288 of 1911-12 and order was passed therein on 26-3-1912 for demarcation of the lands settled in favour of Aparna Charan and accordingly, demarcation was made by an Amin of the said office on 26-3-1912 and since the creation of the said jote Aparna Charan had been in exclusive possession of the suit property and he had brick fields therein as well as the adjoining lands and during RS operation major portion of the said Jote No. 88/88 was recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 as RS Jote No. 81 and by mistake the remaining portion, i.e. the suit property comprising of RS Plot No, 2956 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 776, was wrongly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala as RS Jote No. 86 though he had no title or possession therein and that the defendant No. 1, after death of his father in the year 1929, had also been in continuous possession thereof over the statutory period of limitation and also used the suit land as a part of his brick field and after coming to know that the bank wrongly entered its name in the RS record in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37, filed an application praying for mutation of his name upon correction of the aforesaid wrong entry in the name of the bank and the said application to the Khashmohal Office, Sadar, Chittagong, was registered as JM Case No. 230A/11 of 1554-55 and then notice was duly served upon the bank and in spite of receiving the notice the bank, having no interest in the suit property, did not contest the said application and then the right, title, interest and possession of the defendant No. 1 being found in Jote No. 86 after proper enquiry, by order dated 30-3-1955 the suit property, along with other properties, were recorded in the name of the defendant No. 1 and as far back as 1959 he sold a part of the suit land measuring 1.20 acres to Pakistan Tobacco Co Ltd, the predecessor in interest of Bangladesh Tobacco Co Ltd, the defendant No. 3, who after enjoying the said property till 1964 disposed of the same in favour of State Bank of Pakistan, the predecessor of Bangladesh Bank, the defendant No. 4, whose name has been duly recorded in the record of rights and who is in possession of the same by paying rents regularly; the defendant No. 5 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of his purchase from a subsequent transferee of the defendant No. 1 and the proforma defendant No. 6 is in possession of part of the suit property by virtue of direct purchase from the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 1 has made similar transfers from the suit property to various other purchasers and they, after constructing pucca buildings on portions of the suit property so purchased are in possession of the same long over the statutory period of limitation openly and adversely and since they were not made parties, the suit is bad for defect of parties and neither Sarada Kripa Lala nor the bank had ever any possession, right, title or interest in the suit property. 

 5. The defendant No. 2 also contested the suit and filed separate affidavit-in-opposition contending that Sarada Kripa Lala never mortgaged the suit property to the bank the suit property did not become the subject matter of the mortgage suit as well as the execution case and that the suit property was rightly recorded in the name of Sarada Kripa Lala during RS operation wherein his status has been recorded as a sthitiban raiyat and he on 4-3-29, made a will bequeathing the suit jote to Madhabi Lata Lala, his daughter-in-law, who, on 17-12-1940 after obtaining probate in Probate Suit No. 4 of 1939 was in continuous and uninterrupted possession of the same on payment of rent and she, after obtaining per-mission from the concerned authority under section 9 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and also obtaining Income Tax Clearance Certificates, sold the suit jote to the defendant No. 2 by kabala dated 29-9-1958 and thus the defendant No. 2 became the absolute owner in possession of the suit jote and his title has also been perfected by lapse of time and that the defendant No. 1, having fraudulently got his name mutated in RS Jote No. 86 and resisted the mutation of the name of this defendant and also the possession of the defendant No. 2 in the suit jote, he filed Other Class Suit No. 49 of  1959 for declaration of his title in the suit jote and also for recovery of khas possession which being dismissed he preferred First Appeal No. 115 of 1965 before the High Court, Dhaka which is pending. 

 "With regard to the oral evidence on possession, PW 1 Md Shahjahan has stated that he joined Bangladesh Bank only in April, 1981. He has deposed with reference to the papers and documents available to him. He has no personal knowledge about possession. Therefore the plaintiff's case on adverse possession in based on documentary evidence only." 

 Exhibit 5 is the next document relied upon my Dr M Zahir. It is the certified copy of the proceeding of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43. It appears from the compensation schedule that RS Plot No. 2956 was requisitioned by the land Acquisition Department during the World War II in the said LA Case and occupied by the Military authorities on 30-11-1942. It also shows that the Mahluxmi Bank Ltd, was entered in the compensation schedule as the owner in possession of RS Plot No. 2956  ..... That finding recording the contemporaneous possession of the Bank remains a strong piece of evidence in favour of the plaintiff unchallenged subsequently by Sarada Kripa Lala. He or any one also claiming through him did not file any suit challenging the recording of RS Plot No. 2956 in favour of the Mahaluxmi Bank Ltd, as far back as in 1936. Although it is quite probable that the bank took possession of the suit plot on 24-10-1932 when it took possession of the other mortgaged properties of Sarada Kripa Lala, I shall not go by probabilities, but evidence. I shall take Exhibit 4 as the evidence of contemporaneous maters, not as an evidence of matters past. I have also taken note of the fact that Exhibit 4 remains unchallenged by the defendants. It has also not been assailed on any ground whatsoever." 

 12. Leave was granted on the submissions that the defendant No. 1 transferred the major portion of the suit property to others long before the institution of the instant suit and those transferees having not been impleaded inspite of objection taken and, as such, the suit is bad for defect of parties and the High Court Division, upon an erroneous view, held that since those transferees will stand or fall with the defendant No. 1; the learned Single Judge having found that the bank was not a mortgagee in respect of the suit property and that the suit land was wrongly mutated in the name of the bank as a mortgagee in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and that "the actual mutation as a mortgagee in possession does not also reflect the correct position" and there having been absolutely no oral evidence of possession by the bank, committed grave error of law in finding title of the bank by adverse possession on the basis of the order of mutation of the suit property in the above JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 specially when in their pleading the bank did not plead that they acquired title adverse possession; there having been no evidence whatsoever of the bank's entering into possession of the suit property the learned Single Judge was manifestly wrong in holding that the correct position was that the bank entered into possession of the suit property mistakenly as a mortgagee and such a finding is solely based on surmise and conjecture; even if it is assumed for argument's sake, without however conceding that the plaintiff bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936, the learned Single Judge failed to notice that the bank claiming to have entered in possession as a mortgagee and having neither pleaded nor adduced evidence to show from when the plaintiff asserted absolute title to the disputed land;, the defendant No. 1 having examined a number of person to prove his possession in the suit property and there having been no evidence adduced by either the bank or defendant No. 2 in support of this adverse possession, the learned Single Judge ought to have held that the defendant No. 1, all through, had been in possession of the suit property; the learned Single Judge misread Exhibit 5, the certified copy of the proceedings of Land Acquisition of LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 to find possession of the bank, inasmuch as Exhibit 5 neither shows that possession of the suit property was taken from the bank nor shows that the said property was redelivered to the bank upon de-requisition and even if it is assumed for argument's sake without however conceding that the bank was in possession of the suit property prior to 30-11-1942, when the government took possession of the same the bank being a trespasser could not tack the period between 30-11-1942 and 38-1-1947 for acquisition of title by adverse possession, inasmuch as the government having taken over possession of the suit property under the law, the possession of the bank was snapped and fresh period of limitation would start to run from the time the suit property was derequisitioned and vacated by the government, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt taken together with other documents clearly establish that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation, and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property and failed to consider that the documents produced by him and particularly, the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 and also shows that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis, the learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession, whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned in 1947; the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff to, prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and, in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955; the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. 

 13. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the appellant, in his submission reiterated the grounds as stated above and also submitted that the High Court Division fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was sub-divided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map, and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy. 

 14. Mr Shafiq Ahmed, the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1, submitted that although plea of adverse possession was not raised in the pleading but issue No. 6 specifically related to adverse possession and the defendants led evidence in this regard and before the witnesses were examined the learned Advocate for the bank made oral submission that the bank would claim title by adverse as well and the learned Advocate for the defendants did not oppose the above submission and argued that the defendant No. 1 failed to establish his adverse possession on the suit property by adequate evidence and, in view of the above, the High Court Division was competent in considering the case of adverse possession in the light of entire evidence on record and on consideration of evidence on record, particularly order sheet of JM Case No. 234 of 1936-37, Exhibit 4 the High Court Division rightly came to the finding that the bank entered into possession of the suit property in the year 1936 on the basis of order dated 7-11-36 passed in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 and continued its possession till 1955 and the Government took over possession of the suit property on 30-11-1942 in LA Case No. 62 of 1942-43 and then the same was returned to the bank on 8-1-47 and the period in which the suit land was under the occupation of the military has been rightly construed by the learned Single Judge to be the possession of the bank and further Exhibit 8, the judgment passed In Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979, was rightly considered by the High Court Division in deciding the suit and the defendant No. 1, as DW 8, in his evidence clearly stated that his father Apama Charan took settlement of some land including the suit land in the year 1907 and the quantum of land was 36 acres but Exhibit A series showed that the total area of land alleged to have been settled was 64.32 acres and, as such, the above discrepancy falsify the above claim of the defendant No. 1 of taking settlement of 36 acres of land by Aparna Charan and further DW 8 in his deposition clearly stated that he has no documentary evidence regarding taking possession of the suit property prior to 1955 except his oral evidence and the other witnesses in support of possession of the defendant No. 1 having contradicted each other in material points, the possession of the defendant No. 1, since taking alleged settlement by his father in 1907, remained not proved and the defendant No. 1 also admitted that neither his father nor himself mutated their name before 1955 and, as such, the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in decreeing the suit. 

 20. In 14 ILR the plaintiff sued to recover possession of certain land, alleging that it was lakhiraj land, which he had purchased from a third party and the Court of first instance having found that he had not proved the title he alleged but proved twelve years' possession decreed the suit. On appeal, the lower appellate Court having found that though 12 years adverse possession had been proved but since acquisition of title by adverse possession was not alleged in the plaint and no issue was raised as to it, the plaintiff was not entitled to succeed. But on appeal the High Court held that as the suit was one for possession and the defendant had express notice in the lower appellate Court that the plaintiff relied on the title of adverse possession, and as the defendant took no objection on the ground that he should be allowed an opportunity to call evidence to rebut it, and as he had consequently not been prejudiced by the course adopted by the lower Appellate Court, the decree of trial Court should be confirmed. 

 25. In the case of Mahaprabhu Ram vs Gopal Ram 42 DLR (AD) 154 referred to by Mr Islam the case of the appellants was one of acquisition of title by settlement which was not proved on trial and the trial Court conferred title on him on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession, unwarranted by pleading. The High Court Division held that the gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition and that of the precise title to which the plaintiff lays his claim is not supported by evidence on record, the Court cannot find out another source of title for him, by way of gratuitous relief. 

 26. In the case of Gouri Das vs ABM Hasan Kabir 7 BLC (AD) 140 referred to by Mr Islam, argument of adverse possession was advanced submitting that in the terms of section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 a tenant must show that he had been holding the property in question for a period of not less than 12 years without any lease and this Division held that mere suggestion of uninterrupted possession for 12 years or that the plaintiff had acquired an absolute title is not enough and to claim adverse possession it must be specifically pleaded in the plaint and hostile title must be asserted and the adverse possession must be adequate in continuity and furthermore, evidence must be adduced to show when possession became adverse so that the starting point of limitation against the party affected can be found and in the instant appeal, there was no attempt to prove since when the adverse possession has started and there is no evidence when possession became adverse and that long possession is not necessarily adverse possession. 

 31. In 38 ILR it was held that a person could not acquire a title by adverse possession to land which was the subject of a usufructuary mortgage and therefore in the possession of the mortgagees, merely because he had managed to get his name recorded in the village papers for a series of years in respect of the mortgage property and it must be borne in mind that the equity of redemption where the possession remains with the mortgagor is quite different from the equity of redemption where the possession is with the mortgagee and there can be no doubt that an equitable estate, as distinguished from a legal estate, can be barred by time but it seems to us impossible that any person can be in possession of the right to redeem a mortgage where, under the terms of the mortgage, the mortgagee is entitled to the actual possession, and is in fact in possession thereunder. 

 42. In the case of Hemanta Kumari Debi vs Midnapore Zemindary Co Ltd AIR 1942 (Calcutta) 233 referred by Mr Islam it was held that when the defendant in possession sets up a title only to a limited interest which even if completed would not extinguish the title of the plaintiff and it is for the defendant to establish his title in order to defeat the claim of the plaintiff and the extent of the title acquired by adverse possession depends on the extent of the claim or right under which possession is obtained and kept and if the claim is restricted to a limited interest in the property, e.g. tenancy right in the property, possession is adverse to the extent of that limited interest only and there can be no question of absolute title by adverse possession when only a limited interest has been asserted. In the present case, the bank mutated its name in the suit property that is in JM Case No. 236 of 1936-37 as a mortgagee, that is, on the basis of limited interest and since the learned Single Judge held that the bank was not a mortgagee and also did not purchase the suit property in auction the bank as is evident from Exhibit 00 held the suit property for its control and management, which means with the consent of Sarada Kripa Lala. 

 45. Further, Exhibit A series, i.e. the proceedings of Boundary Demarcation Miscellaneous Case No. 288 of 1911-12 and Exhibit N, the rent receipt, taken together with other documents established that Aparna Charan, the father of the defendant No. 1, took settlement of the entire CS Plot No. 1748 of which the suit property was a part and he possessed the same until his death in the year 1929, before RS operation and the learned Single Judge upon untenable ground disbelieved the case of the defendant No. 1 claiming title to the entire CS Plot No. 1748 including the suit property. The learned Single Judge also failed to consider that the documents produced by the defendant No. 1, particularly the records of Exhibit A series and the map prepared by the Amin therein, clearly established the claim of the defendant No. 1 in the suit property and also show that the entry of the name of Sarada Kripa Lala in the RS record of rights is completely without basis. The learned Single Judge on the basis of Report of JM Case No. 230A/ 11 of 1954-55, having found Exhibit R(1), that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property in the year 1955 and the defendant No. 1 adduced oral evidence in support of his possession whereas there having been no evidence as to how the bank came into possession of the suit property, ought to have held that the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the suit property ever since it was derequisitioned on 8-1-1947 and the present proceeding being for recovery of possession the burden of proof was on the bank, the plaintiff, to prove its possession and the bank having failed to adduce any evidence in this regard the defendant No. 1 was not required to adduce any evidence of possession and in this state of affairs, when the preponderance of evidence regarding possession was heavily in favour of the defendant No. 1, the learned Single Judge ignoring the preponderance of evidence, wrongly found that the defendant No. 1 was not in possession of the suit property prior to 1955. Further, the finding of the learned Single Judge that Aparna Charan did not take settlement of the entire CS plot No. 1748 and that Sarada Kripa Lala was in possession of the suit property at the time of RS operation and that the defendant No. 1 failed to rebut the presumption of the RS record of rights and the defendant No. 1 went into possession of the suit property taking advantage of the moribund condition of the bank are all contrary to the evidence on record and are the result of surmise and conjecture. It also appears that the learned Single Judge fell in error in relying on Exhibit AA, alleged traced copy of the CS map, to hold that CS Plot No. 1748 was subdivided before RS Operation, inasmuch as Exhibit AA is only a traced copy and there is no evidence on record to show that any competent authority passed any order to treat Exhibit AA as an original CS map and specially when it does not satisfy the requirement of section 83 of the Evidence Act and further, the High Court Division also fell in error in not taking into consideration the judgment and order passed in Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1979 as being not inter parties without considering that the said judgment and order, though not inter parties, was admissible under section 13 of the Evidence Act to prove the fact that the relevant original CS map along with a traced copy was filed in that suit and no division or Bata-dags were shown in the original CS map while such division was shown in the traced copy.
